meta.book: Javier Fernández-Sebastián, Key Metaphors for History: Mirrors of Time (Routledge, 2024)
meta.method: deterministic markdown parse + curated analytical enrichment
meta.notes: 3.3.4 Shards accepted as an explicit class from the 2024 book. Existing model label indices remain unchanged; the new class is appended at global index 43 in the training JSON.

families.paraphrased_description: Metaphors through which history reflects on itself as knowledge and craft: as a mirror of truth, a construction, a teacher, the transfigured muse Clio, a tribunal, or a bordered territory.
families.source_domain: reflexive imagery of the discipline itself (optics, building, teaching, myth, law, territory)
families.historical_function: figures historians use to picture what history *is* and what writing history does

families.paraphrased_description: Metaphors that render time and memory imaginable: the muses Chronos/Kairos, circles and lines, rivers and seas, atmospheres, geological strata, turbulence, and the modern flood of memory.
families.historical_function: images that give shape to historical time and to collective memory

families.paraphrased_description: Metaphors articulating how past, present, and future relate: the essential triad, the past as a foreign country or a tomb, the future as light, seed, or horizon.
families.source_domain: lived time, geography, death/burial, light, botany, the horizon
families.historical_function: images for the mutual relations of the three temporal ekstases

families.paraphrased_description: Metaphors built into core methodological concepts: sources one drinks from, events as surface foam vs. established facts, and history as deep process or structure.
families.source_domain: springs/fountains, surface phenomena, nature and music
families.historical_function: metaphors underpinning the technical vocabulary of historical method

families.paraphrased_description: Metaphors that animate modern temporal concepts: revolution as runaway vehicle, crisis as decisive turning point, and the many self-images of modernity from the invisible hand to the runaway engine.
families.source_domain: vehicles and forces, medicine, cosmology, wind/storm, networks, machines
families.historical_function: metaphors organizing the master temporal concepts of modernity

families.definition: All these terms derive from a handful of Latin verbs: *progredi* (to walk forward), *clinare/declinare* (to bend; to bend downward), *cadere/decadere* (to fall), *transire* (to go across), and *tradere* (to deliver, hand down). (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 219; cf. Nisbet 1969, 242–243, 271–272).
families.paraphrased_description: Directional metaphors derived from verbs of walking, bending, falling, crossing, and handing down: progress and development, decadence and decline, tradition and transition.
families.source_domain: Latin verbs of motion: progredi, declinare, cadere, transire, tradere
families.historical_function: directional metaphors for the overall movement of history

entries.paraphrased_description: History pictured as a mirror that reflects the past (and even the future), associated with the image of naked truth.
entries.source_domain: optics / reflection (mirror, glass)
entries.historical_function: history as a faithful reflection of truth and of the past
example_patterns: history is the mirror of the past
short_evidence_snippets: “[…] the mirror of history has been associated with an image no less full of meaning: that of the naked truth.” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 23).
“[…] history is ‘the mirror of the past, guide of the present, lighthouse of the future’.” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 25).
“[…] ‘history is the mirror in which the past reflects the future […]’.” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 25).

entries.paraphrased_description: History as a multifaceted object to be examined from many sides; knowledge tied to a vantage point (Gadamer's range of vision).
entries.source_domain: vision / viewpoint (vantage point, angle)
entries.historical_function: historical knowledge as bound to a situated perspective
short_evidence_snippets: “[…] that history is ‘a multifaceted column,’ which should be examined by the researcher ‘on all its sides’.” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 31).
“The range of vision that includes everything that can be seen from a particular vantage point.” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 31).

entries.paraphrased_description: The historian's work as creation and construction, not discovery or recovery (Oakeshott).
entries.source_domain: building / making (construction, architecture)
entries.historical_function: history as something the historian constructs rather than merely finds
short_evidence_snippets: “The historian’s business is not to discover, to recapture, or even to interpret; it is to create and to construct.” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 32).

entries.paraphrased_description: History as master and teacher — mother of truth, witness and counsel — yet also the ironic lesson that nothing is learned from it.
entries.source_domain: pedagogy (teaching, mastery; historia magistra vitae)
entries.historical_function: history as teacher and store of exemplary lessons
short_evidence_snippets: “What experience and history teach is this – that nations and governments have never learned anything from history, or acted upon any lessons they might have drawn from it.” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 32).
“History as the mother of truth, ‘rival of time, storehouse of deeds, witness for the past, example and counsel for the present, and warning for the future’.” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 34).

entries.paraphrased_description: The classical muse Clio recast in modern guise — the umbrella for trains, motion, and tribunal imagery that secularizes and dynamizes history.
entries.source_domain: mythology reconfigured (the muse Clio made modern)
entries.historical_function: the personified muse of history transfigured into modern, dynamic forms
short_evidence_snippets: “The task of history, once the other-world of truth has vanished, is to establish the truth of this world.” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 37).

entries.paraphrased_description: The train of time, railway of progress, and locomotive of history — and the revolution reimagined as the emergency brake.
entries.source_domain: rail transport / locomotion (train, railway, locomotive)
entries.historical_function: history/progress/revolution as a locomotive racing forward to make up lost time
short_evidence_snippets: “The train of time, the railway of progress, the locomotive of history – three slightly different versions of the same imagery – travel purposefully forward at great speed, as they have to make up fo…
“History is about the most cruel of all goddesses, and she leads her triumphal car over heaps of corpses, not only in war, but also in ‘peaceful’ economic development.” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 38).
“Maybe the revolution was not actually the locomotive, as Marx maintained, but rather its antithesis: the emergency brake that avoids a catastrophe.” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 39).

entries.paraphrased_description: History in motion — the centaur of philosophy of history, the world-soul on horseback, stallions, masses and revolutionaries in action.
entries.source_domain: motion / animals and vehicles (horses, centaur, triumphal car)
entries.historical_function: history personified as a force or figure in visible movement
short_evidence_snippets: “Prominent among the images applied by its critics to the philosophy of history as such is that of the centaur … This pejorative metaphor emphasizes the monstrous nature of this strange creature, hal…

“The ‘world-soul on horseback’ that Hegel thought he saw going down the street in front of his house in Jena is easier to imagine … The Fourth Estate … revolutions of the 20th century in Mexico, Russ…

“Post-revolutionary historiography and romantic painting … were full of spirited stallions, smoking trains, monuments, ruins of the past, masses in movement, and revolutionaries in action.” (SEBASTIÁ…

“A painting by John Gast, *American Progress*, shows how the expansion brought the light of civilization … telegraph wire and a school book … railway line that enabled communication and transportatio…

entries.paraphrased_description: History as the world's court of justice that will judge or absolve actors — and conversely as the dustbin into which the past is thrown.
entries.source_domain: law and waste (tribunal, court of justice; dustbin, rubbish)
entries.historical_function: history as moral tribunal that judges and absolves, or as a dustbin discarding the past
short_evidence_snippets: “The History of the World is the World’s Court of Justice.” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 42).
“My name already belongs to history: she will judge me.” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 43).
“History will absolve me!” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 44).
“History will judge me, but just to be safe, I shall choose the historians.” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 45).

entries.paraphrased_description: Counter-metaphors that turn the tables — life that must judge history; the Angel of History seeing progress as a heap of rubble.
entries.source_domain: critical inversion (Nietzsche's life over history; Benjamin's Angel)
entries.historical_function: metaphors that contest the idealization and authority of History/progress
short_evidence_snippets: “Life that must judge history.” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 46).
“The Angel of History denounces the outrage of progress and repudiates the glories once sung by the muse, which for the angel have been reduced to a heap of rubble.” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 50).

entries.paraphrased_description: History mapped as a territory with porous borders to philosophy, rhetoric, theology, geography and politics — subject to 'turns' and lacking natural frontiers.
entries.source_domain: territory and boundaries (borders, fields, professions, turns)
entries.historical_function: history as a domain with shifting borders and turns among neighbouring disciplines
short_evidence_snippets: “It should be borne in mind that for centuries no clear borders existed between history and philosophy, rhetoric, theology, morality, geography, philology, literature, or politics – domains which tod…
“The brightest star in the social firmament … a sphere that partly directs other activities and ‘lacks natural borders’.” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 53).

entries.class_label: Memory of Time / Time of Memory
entries.paraphrased_description: Time and memory caught in mutual implication — as in expressions where the thing (wind, river, time) seems separable from its very movement.
entries.source_domain: substance vs. process (wind blows, river flows, time passes)
entries.historical_function: the reflexive entanglement of time and memory
short_evidence_snippets: “Phrases such as ‘the wind blows,’ ‘the river flows,’ or ‘time passes’ seem to suggest that the wind, the river, or time was something substantially different from their movement — the act of blowing…

entries.paraphrased_description: Clio writing on the back of Chronos; time the devourer against memory the preserver; the fullness or ripeness of Kairos.
entries.source_domain: mythology (Clio, Chronos the devourer, Kairos the opportune moment)
entries.historical_function: tension between recording memory, devouring linear time, and the ripe moment
short_evidence_snippets: Clio is often shown writing on Chronos’ back (17th–18th c.) (Fernández-Sebastián 2021c; SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 63).
The destructive power of Chronos (“time the devourer”) contrasts with Clio’s preserving mission. Herodotus wrote that he aimed “that time does not abolish men’s achievements and to ensure that their…
Sculpture in Wiblingen Abbey shows Clio halting Chronos as he tries to tear out a page of history, symbolizing the struggle between memory and time (Ricoeur 2004).
“Time the destroyer is time the preserver.” (T. S. Eliot, *Four Quartets*).

entries.paraphrased_description: Time figured through shapes: classical cycles vs. Christian linearity, the point of eternity or the messianic instant, and the spiral.
entries.source_domain: geometry (circle, line, point, spiral)
entries.historical_function: the figural shape of time — cyclical, linear, punctual, or spiral
short_evidence_snippets: Classical cyclical vs. Christian linear time (Augustine, *City of God*). (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 64).
Eternity as non-time; Gnostic interruptions; messianic expectations; spiral time (Latour 1993; SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 65).
Indigenous Colombian spiral conception (Rappaport 2003).
Spanish Jesuit Nieremberg’s *Treatise on the Difference Between the Temporal and the Eternal* (1640).

entries.paraphrased_description: One of the oldest images of time: the river that flows yet endures (Heraclitus), the sea of language and understanding, the historian as boatman on the stream of time.
entries.source_domain: hydrology (river, stream, current, sea, ocean)
entries.historical_function: time/history as flowing water — continuity within change
short_evidence_snippets: The river as one of the oldest metaphors of time — fluid yet continuous — recalling Heraclitus. (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 67).
“All social reality came to be seen as a historical stream or river.” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 67).
“The story is our only boat for sailing on the river of time.” — Ursula K. Le Guin, *A Fisherman of the Inland Sea* (1994).
Ricoeur: narrative as the “guardian of time.” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 67).

entries.paraphrased_description: A period figured as an enveloping atmosphere or spiritual climate — the spirit of the age, the air one breathes, the threshold between climates.
entries.source_domain: meteorology / air (atmosphere, climate, Zeitgeist)
entries.historical_function: an epoch as a pervasive atmosphere one breathes
short_evidence_snippets: “History, with the Annales, flowed out of the river of time and settled into an atmospheric inertia.” (Marlon Salomon 2018a, 149).
Febvre viewed the 16th-century Christian world as an “atmosphere” enveloping all — not merely a set of beliefs. (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 72–73).
Expressions like *genius saeculi*, *Zeitgeist*, and “spirit of the age” prefigured the metaphor of atmosphere. (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 73).
“Democracy is the principle of these times… present in the atmosphere we live in, in the air we breathe.” — Ordax Avecilla, *Diario de Sesiones*, 16 Dec 1854.

entries.paraphrased_description: Historical time stratified into surface events and deep, slow structures — Unamuno's intrahistory, Braudel's longue durée, Koselleck's layers of time.
entries.source_domain: geology (strata, sediment, seabed, layers)
entries.historical_function: a layered, depth model of historical time
short_evidence_snippets: Unamuno compared daily life to the “sea of history,” where surface events are waves above deep intrahistory. (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 75).
“The almost motionless seabed constitutes true, universal, and everlasting tradition.” (*En torno al casticismo*, 1895).
Braudel distinguished surface “evental” waves from deep structural time, slow as nature’s rhythms. (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 75).
Löwith likened surface turmoil to waves over a silent sea-bed. (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 75).

entries.paraphrased_description: Time as turbulent flow and as shattered fragments — currents dragging us off, shards cutting the mind, palimpsests and folds.
entries.source_domain: turbulence and shattering (whirl, shards, washing machine)
entries.historical_function: chaotic, fragmented, accelerated temporality
short_evidence_snippets: “Turbulence brings us back to the metaphorics of flow… furious currents that drag us to unknown destinations.” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 78).
“It is like the glass front of a washing machine…” (Koselleck 2004b, 260).
“Time was splintered… shards cutting into your mind.” — Ruth Kluger, *Weiter leben* (1992); *Still Alive* (2001).
“The creator of allegories works with shards.” (Kittsteiner 1996, 61).

entries.paraphrased_description: The memory boom as a trickle swelling into a flood and a sea; sites of memory as shells left when the sea recedes; inscription as sowing.
entries.source_domain: flood + inscription (trickle to flood; wax tablet, aviary)
entries.historical_function: the late-20th-century memory boom figured as a rising deluge
short_evidence_snippets: “Over the course of the 1980s, an initial trickle of writing on history and memory became a flood.” (Megill 1998, 43).
“When we first conceived cultural memory… it was then a small river; today, it has grown into a sea.” (Assmann 2011, xi).
“The sites of memory are like shells left on the shore when the sea of living memory has receded.” (Hartog 2015, 126).
Plato’s metaphors: the wax tablet (imprint) and the aviary (storage of thoughts) initiated durable memory imagery. (*Phaedrus*; *Theaetetus*).

entries.paraphrased_description: The essential triad: each present contains a past, a present, and a future — the knot tying time's dimensions together.
entries.source_domain: lived time (three 'todays'; knot/bundle)
entries.historical_function: every historical present binds together three distinct times
short_evidence_snippets: “Every historic present involves three distinct times, three different ‘todays’.” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 99).
“The past is a previous future and a recent present, the present is an impending past and a recent future, and finally, the future is a present and even a past to come.” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 99).

“A certain romantic view of history envisioned Europe as the present, inheritor of a past that was connected to Asia, and seeking young America as a reflection of its future.” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 99…

entries.paraphrased_description: Past and present in mutual definition — history as a 'science of the present' that connects what is otherwise unconnected.
entries.source_domain: relational time (connection of presents)
entries.historical_function: the past exists for the sake of, and through, the present
short_evidence_snippets: “The character of the past is that it connects what is unconnected in the merging of one present into another.” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 105).
“History is about the past for the sake of the present.” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 105).

“Ortega y Gasset insisted time and time again that the past and the future only exist in the present. The present would be the knot that ties in a bundle the other two dimensions of time, in such a w…

entries.paraphrased_description: The past as a foreign country where they do things differently — naming both the deep cut from the present and the urge to stitch it closed.
entries.source_domain: geography / travel (a foreign country abroad)
entries.historical_function: the alterity of the past and the modern wish to suture the cut
example_patterns: the past is a foreign country
short_evidence_snippets: “The past is a foreign country, and, as Hartley wrote, ‘they do things differently there.’” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 107).

“In this metaphor, of which there are several variants, lies the gist of the modern idea of history, which acknowledges the existence of a deep cut between the present and the past and at the same ti…

entries.paraphrased_description: History as a tomb that lays the dead past to rest in scriptural graves; or, against that, the past living on in spectral form.
entries.source_domain: death and burial (tomb, corpse, ghost, decay)
entries.historical_function: history as burial of the dead past — or as its ghostly survival
short_evidence_snippets: “History is a tomb for the corpse past, insofar as it allows society to draw a line between what is dead and what is not, calming the dead who still haunt the present by offering them scriptural tomb…
“Instead of the metaphor of past-dead, she recommends that the past should continue living in the present, albeit in ghostly form.” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 110).

“Far beneath its surface, the struggles of history, long dead, worked their powerful chemistry: here were the corpses of feudalism and absolutism, in various stages of decay; here were the ashes of h…

entries.paraphrased_description: Distances and dimensions of time — the historian ascends from the present toward origins; retrospection is a double-edged sword risking the condescension of posterity.
entries.source_domain: spatial distance / optics (ascent, descent, retrospect)
entries.historical_function: the historian's retrospective vantage and its hazards
short_evidence_snippets: “The real succession of events descends from the origin down to their most recent ordering; the universal historian ascends from the most recent world situation upwards toward the origin of things.”…

“We understand then that the historian’s ‘secret weapon’ is a double-edged sword. Retrospectiveness is certainly an advantage, but it involves the risk of misinterpreting past events and incurring in…

entries.paraphrased_description: Present and future — the present as window, watchtower, blind spot or trap from which the empirically unverifiable future is glimpsed.
entries.source_domain: verifiability and vision (open window, watchtower, eye of the hurricane)
entries.historical_function: the present's vantage onto an unverifiable future
short_evidence_snippets: “Past events are contained in our experience and are empirically verifiable. What is to come is fundamentally beyond our experience and, as such, is not empirically verifiable.” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p.…

“A permanently open window in a moving vehicle or a watchtower on a mountain-top, but also that of the eye of the hurricane, that of a kind of blind spot from which you cannot see your own eyeball, t…

entries.paraphrased_description: Lights — the past as a lamp at the entrance to the future; the guiding star of progress that may have ceased to shine (a dead star).
entries.source_domain: light / illumination (lamp, star, beacon, darkness)
entries.historical_function: the past or reason illuminating the future
short_evidence_snippets: “The past is like a lamp placed at the entrance to the future, to dispel some of the darkness that covers it.” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 120).
“The past had ceased to throw its light upon the future, and consequently the mind of man wandered in obscurity.” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 120).
“It is highly symptomatic in this respect that the future is sometimes metaphorized as a dead star – the guiding star of enlightened and positivist modernity would have ceased to shine.” (SEBASTIÁN,…

entries.paraphrased_description: Seeds — agricultural and obstetric images: the present as seed, bud, or pregnancy of a coming future; revolution as birth and the midwife of a new society.
entries.source_domain: botany / generation (seed, bud, flower, harvest, pregnancy)
entries.historical_function: the present as the seed or bud of a future yet to germinate
example_patterns: the bud of a future flower
short_evidence_snippets: “Every century carries in it the seed of the events that will unfold in the ensuing century.” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 121).
“Our Humanity is only preparation, the bud of a future flower.” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 122).
“Under corruption, future good will germinate, as good seed germinates under manure.” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 123).

entries.paraphrased_description: Horizons — the future as an open, advancing horizon line; Koselleck's horizon of expectation (Erwartungshorizont) and Gadamer's fusion of horizons (Horizontverschmelzung); a later vertical sense links horizon to geological strata.
entries.source_domain: geography / vision of the horizon (and, later, geological 'horizons'/strata)
entries.historical_function: the future and the historicity of understanding figured as a moving, expanding horizon
entries.page_reference_note: Approximate printed pages; recovered from book body rather than from the curated source.

“every living thing can become healthy, strong and fruitful only within a horizon.” (Nietzsche, 1874; recovered from book body)
Koselleck's horizon of expectation [Erwartungshorizont] and Gadamer's fusion of horizons [Horizontverschmelzung].
entries.uncertainty_note: The source `metaphors_javier.md` truncates mid-3.3.3 ('Every living thing can become healthy, strong, and fruitful only with…'). Description and cues recovered from the book body (Ch. 3, 'Present and future'): Nietzsche's '…only within a horizon', plus Koselleck and Gadamer.

entries.paraphrased_description: Sources and traces — historians 'drink' from sources that may be pure or contaminated, abundant or drying up; memory as a heap of broken fragments.
entries.source_domain: springs / fountains and traces (water source, fragments)
entries.historical_function: historical evidence figured as sources one drinks from and as traces
short_evidence_snippets: “For instance, historians supposedly drink or feed from historical sources — sources that, as the case may be, might be abundant and inexhaustible but also insufficient, drying up, and disappearing.…

“The primitive ‘source’ does not consist in the dreary maze of contemporary opinions, accounts, reports. This is only the daily repeated atmospheric process of ascending and self-precipitating vapors…
“The memory of the world is not a bright, shining crystal, but a heap of broken fragments, a few fine flashes of light that break through the darkness.” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 137).

entries.paraphrased_description: Events and facts — events as surface foam and crests carried by the tides of history, or as a 'black hole' of meaning; facts as established constructions.
entries.source_domain: surface phenomena (foam, crests, black hole)
entries.historical_function: the distinction between events that happen and facts that are established
short_evidence_snippets: “Events happen, facts are established.” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 142).
“An event would be a ‘black hole’ of meaning, as the Holocaust has been referred to.” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 143).
“Surface disturbances, crests of foam that the tides of history carry on their strong backs.” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 145).

entries.paraphrased_description: Processes and structures — the event as a single note on the keyboard of structure; history as natural process: waves, glacial drift, tectonic movement, alluvial deposit.
entries.source_domain: nature and music (keyboard, waves, glacial drift, tectonics)
entries.historical_function: history as deep process and structure beneath the events
short_evidence_snippets: “A historian worthy of the name must represent every event as part of an entirety.” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 150).
“History [understood here as structure] is the keyboard on which these individual notes [i.e., the events] are sounded.” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 152).
“History then becomes a process in nature, a sequence of waves, a glacial drift, a tectonic fault movement, a flood, or an alluvial deposit.” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 153).

entries.paraphrased_description: Revolution figured as a careering carriage rushing from precipice to precipice, a brake against speeding culture, or supra-gigantic forces crushing or carrying individuals.
entries.source_domain: vehicles and forces (carriage, locomotive, brake, supra-gigantic forces)
entries.historical_function: revolution as runaway vehicle or overwhelming force dragging humanity
short_evidence_snippets: “We jumped aboard the carriage of the revolution, and dragged from precipice to precipice, in a few hours we completed the journey that should have taken many years.” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 175).
“Sometimes a culture is in the greatest need of a brake: namely, when it is going too fast downhill or, as in the present case perhaps, too fast uphill.” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 176).

“Supra-gigantic forces whose movements race through humanity, dragging every individual willy-nilly with them – either riding atop their triumphant car or crushed under its wheels.” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024,…

entries.paraphrased_description: Crisis as the great divide bridging one epoch and another, a nexus of growth reached by leaps, a moment of change that lights up all levels of social reality.
entries.source_domain: medicine / turning point / bridge (crisis, growth-nexus, epoch-bridge)
entries.historical_function: crisis as a decisive turning point that illuminates an epoch
short_evidence_snippets: “We stand in the middle of the kind of great crisis that bridges the gap between one epoch and another, a crisis that resembles that of the Crusades, that of the era of Reformation, when America appe…
“All spiritual growth takes place by leaps and bounds, both in the individual and in the community. The crisis is to be regarded as a new nexus of growth.” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 187).
“Moment of change which sheds light on all the elements of social formation, and all the levels of reality.” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 190).

entries.paraphrased_description: Modernity — the parent grouping for the family of metaphors by which the modern age pictures itself (revelation, hidden agency, rationalization, storm, contract, network, machine).
entries.source_domain: umbrella for modern self-imagery (multiple source domains)
entries.historical_function: grouping node for the self-images of the modern age

entries.paraphrased_description: Revelation, discovery, disappointment — Copernican and cosmological discovery empties the universe of meaning, turning it into a silent galactic desert and decentring humanity.
entries.source_domain: cosmology / discovery (Copernican decentering, galactic desert)
entries.historical_function: modernity as disenchanting revelation and consequent disappointment
short_evidence_snippets: “The historical reception of Copernicus’s theories and the subsequent cosmological discoveries deprived the universe of its metaphysical content, transformed it into an immense silent and indifferent…

entries.paraphrased_description: Action and mastery — history moved by concealed hands: Smith's invisible hand, Kant's ruse of nature, Hegel's cunning of reason.
entries.source_domain: hidden agency (invisible hand, ruse of nature, cunning of reason)
entries.historical_function: modern history as steered by an impersonal, cunning agency
short_evidence_snippets: “Invisible hand.” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 196).
“Ruse of nature.” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 196).
“Cunning of Reason.” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 196).

entries.paraphrased_description: Rationalization and secularization — the Cartesian light of reason; Foucault's image of 'man' erased like a face drawn in sand at the sea's edge.
entries.source_domain: light and erosion (light of reason; a face erased in sand)
entries.historical_function: modernity as rationalization and secularization
short_evidence_snippets: “Light of reason.” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 196).
“Man would be erased, like a face drawn in sand at the edge of the sea.” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 197).

entries.paraphrased_description: A perennial gale — modernity as ceaseless storm and maelstrom of systems, where the artist must distil the eternal from the transitory.
entries.source_domain: wind and storm (gale, maelstrom, whirlwind)
entries.historical_function: modernity as a perpetual, creative-destructive storm

entries.paraphrased_description: Acceleration — the exponential curve and spiral, Rostow's economic 'take-off', and the paradox of a 'frenetic standstill' or 'frozen time'.

entries.paraphrased_description: Decadence and decline — downward-bending and falling imagery; with the death of meaning in history, the idea of progress dies too.

entries.paraphrased_description: Tradition and transition — tradition as what is handed down (outside which there is only plagiarism); transition as the mind's passage from the absolute to the category of becoming.
entries.source_domain: handing down and crossing over (tradere, transire)
entries.historical_function: tradition as transmission and transition as passage into the historical
short_evidence_snippets: “Outside tradition there is no place for true originality; everything that is not tradition is plagiarism.” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 241).
“The human mind has moved from the absolute to the historical; it now considers everything under the category of becoming.” (SEBASTIÁN, 2024, p. 248).
